Let’s break down each one.

### Myeloma Multiplex (MM)

Also known as **plasmacytoma**, **myelomatosis**, or **Morbus Kahler**, this disease starts in the **bone marrow**—the spongy tissue inside bones where blood cells are made. Specifically, it arises from **plasma cells**, which are a type of white blood cell responsible for producing antibodies.

In MM, these plasma cells become cancerous and multiply uncontrollably. Each tumor forms independently in different parts of the skeleton, which is why the disease is called "multiplex"—it appears in multiple locations. Importantly, these tumors don’t spread from one bone to another like metastases; instead, they arise simultaneously in various marrow-rich sites.

Because the disease originates in the bone marrow itself, it’s considered by most experts to be a **primary bone malignancy**—a cancer that starts in the bone. However, there’s some debate. Ortner and Putschar, for example, classify MM

as a bone tumor but as part of a broader group of disorders affecting the **reticuloendothelial and haemopoietic systems**—the body’s network of immune and blood-forming tissues. This group also includes conditions like leukemia, histiocytosis X, certain anemias, and lipid storage diseases.

So, is MM a bone cancer or a blood cancer? The answer is: **both, in a way**. It’s a cancer of blood-forming cells that happens to grow in the bone and destroy it. This dual nature makes it especially relevant in skeletal analysis.

### Lytic Metastatic Carcinoma (LMC)

Now let’s look at the other major cause of multiple bone holes: **lytic metastatic carcinoma**. This type of cancer starts *outside* the skeleton—usually in an internal organ like the breast, prostate, lung, or thyroid. The cancer begins as a single primary tumor in one of these organs.

Over time, malignant **epithelial cells** (cells that line the surfaces and organs of the body) break away from the original tumor. They enter the bloodstream and travel through the circulatory system—a process called **hematogenous spread**.

When these rogue cells reach the bone, they can settle there and form secondary tumors, known as **metastases**. These metastatic tumors are “lytic,” meaning they dissolve or destroy the surrounding bone tissue, creating the characteristic holes we see in skeletal remains.

Unlike myeloma multiplex, where tumors arise independently in the marrow, metastatic carcinoma spreads from a single source. This difference in origin and spread pattern is crucial—and it can leave different “fingerprints” on the skeleton.

Differential diagnostic conclusions
Many features are common to both MM and LMC. Their incidence is multiple and polytopic, their character is exclusively or predominantly lytic, they originate in the marrow of the cancellous bone, and they progress through erosion of the inner side of the compact bone, undermining, and sometimes slightly lifting, the edge. The range of affected bone is: the vertebrae and sacrum, the ribs and sternum, the pelvis, the skull, and the proximal ends of both the femur and humerus. The lesions occur only rarely distal to the elbow and knee. Pathological fractures — compressions of the vertebrae, multiple transverse breaks of the ribs or long bone fracture — may occur in more advanced cases. Both malignancies have a predilection for individuals of 40 or older.
Combining the experience of various authors with our own, we would like to point out differentiating features.
(i) The density of the lesions is great in MM, whose foci are very numerous and scattered through the skeleton while in LMC the lesions are less numerous and more localized.
(ii) The form of the outline of the lesions is regularly round (circular to slightly oval) in MM, while they are more irregular with denticulations and scallops in LMC.
(iii) The size of the lesions is more consistent, small to medium (up to several milimetres) in
MM, with the exception of foci that merge together. In LMC, their size is more variable, small to large (up to several centimetres).
(iv) Observed macroscopically, the edges of the lesions are sharp and appear as punched-out or bored in MM, while they are scalloped, denticulated or craggy in LMC.
(v) In radiographs, the observed areas of lucidity are clearly and sharply delimited in MM, while they appear obscure, cloudy or 'moth-eaten' in LMC.
(vi) The surface of the surrounding bone is smooth without any pathological change in MM, while it might be pitted with further tiny apertures in LMC, which constitute a zone of potential enlargement of the central lytic lesion through gradual merging.
(vii) The occurrence of an osteoblastic reaction, observable macroscopically at the edges of the lesions or in the trabeculae of the denuded spongiotic bone, as well as radiographically as a zone of increased density around the lesion, is non-existent or extremely slight in quickly progressing MM, while it may be slight or significant in LMC. (viii) A certain topographic predilection was observed by a few investigators. Scapula (glenoid fossa, axillary border and acromion), clavicle (lateral portion), radius and ulna are more typical sites for MM, while the neural arches of the vertebrae and their various processes seems to be more frequently affected in LMC.
(ix) Sexual predilection, deduced from recent statistics, may be applied as well: in MM, males are afflicted twice as often as females, while LMC can be expected to occur more commonly in females, owing especially to longer lasting breast cancer, which did not threaten life in past populations as much as cancers of the important inner organs.
The recent rarity of MM and the common incidence of LMC, quoted by some of the authors, should not be taken as a differential diagnostic criterion because the situation in the past could have been completely different.

Myeloma multiplex versus osteolytic metastatic carcinoma

Let’s begin by painting a clear picture of what was observed in the skeletal remains. Bone lesions—areas where the normal bone structure has been damaged or destroyed—were found in multiple locations across the skeleton. These included the **vertebrae**, **sacrum**, **ribs**, **manubrium sterni** (the upper part of the breastbone), **scapulae** (shoulder blades), **left clavicle** (collarbone), **radius** (one of the two forearm bones), a few **proximal hand phalanges** (the bones of the fingers closest to the hand), and a single **metacarpal** (a bone in the hand). Lesions were also present in both **ossa coxae** (hip bones), and in the **left femur** (thigh bone) and **tibia** (shin bone).

Now, what do these lesions actually look like under the microscope? Histological sections—thin slices of bone tissue prepared for microscopic examination—were made by M. Schultz. These revealed **Howship’s lacunae**. Let’s pause to understand that term.

**What are Howship’s lacunae?**  
These are small, shallow pits or depressions seen on the surface of bone tissue. They are not random damage—they are telltale signs of **osteoclasts** at work. Osteoclasts are specialized cells in the body whose job is to break down bone tissue, a normal part of bone remodeling. But in disease, this process can go into overdrive. When osteoclasts erode bone excessively, they leave behind these little "footprints"—the Howship’s lacunae—indicating active bone destruction. So, their presence here strongly suggests that the lesions are **osteoclastic**, meaning they result from aggressive bone resorption.

The overall character of the bone defects was **predominantly lytic**. Let’s unpack that. A **lytic lesion** is one where bone is being dissolved or destroyed, appearing as "holes" or dark areas on imaging because there’s less dense material. In this case, the lytic areas were accompanied by only a **slight sclerotic reaction**—meaning there was minimal new, dense bone formation around the edges, which the body sometimes uses to wall off damage. This points to a process that is primarily destructive, with little attempt at repair.

How did these lesions develop? They didn’t appear all at once. Instead, they began as **tiny openings** in the bone—like pinpricks of destruction. Over time, these small holes **merged together**, growing into larger perforations. Think of it like small holes in a piece of paper that gradually expand and connect, forming a larger tear. The edges of these lesions were not smooth—they were **uneven, crenulated (scalloped), or frayed**, and surrounded by **minute pores**. This irregular, "ragged" appearance is a clue about the nature of the disease process.

On **radiographs** (X-rays), these lesions appeared **soft**, with **obscure (fuzzy or indistinct) edges**. This is important because different diseases produce different radiographic patterns. A sharp, well-defined edge suggests one kind of process; a blurry, moth-eaten edge suggests another. Here, the fuzziness supports the idea of an aggressive, infiltrative destruction rather than a contained one.

### Differential diagnostic conclusions

Now, we face a critical question: What caused these lesions? Two major possibilities stand out: **Multiple Myeloma (MM)** and **Lytic Metastatic Carcinoma (LMC)**. Both are cancers that can spread to bone and cause lytic lesions. In fact, they share many features, which makes telling them apart a real challenge—especially in ancient skeletal remains where soft tissue is gone and we can’t run modern blood tests or biopsies.

Let’s first look at what **MM and LMC have in common**:

- **Multiple and polytopic**: Lesions appear in many different bones (polytopic), not just one spot.
- **Lytic in character**: Both primarily destroy bone rather than build it up.
- **Origin in marrow**: They start in the **cancellous (spongy) bone**, where bone marrow resides.
- **Progression pattern**: They erode the inner side of the **compact (hard outer) bone**, undermining it—like digging a tunnel beneath a wall until it collapses. Sometimes, this erosion slightly lifts the edge of the cortical bone.
- **Common sites**: Both tend to affect the **axial skeleton**—the vertebrae, sacrum, ribs, sternum, pelvis, and skull—as well as the **proximal ends of long bones** like the femur and humerus.
- **Rare distal involvement**: Lesions are uncommon in bones beyond the elbow or knee.
- **Pathological fractures**: In advanced cases, weakened bones can break. This includes **vertebral compression fractures**, **rib fractures**, or even long bone fractures.
- **Age group**: Both diseases predominantly affect individuals **aged 40 and older**.

Given these similarities, how *can* we tell them apart? By combining insights from various researchers with our own observations, we can identify several **key distinguishing features**.

**(i) Density and distribution of lesions**  
In **Multiple Myeloma (MM)**, the number of lesions is typically **very high**—we’re talking dozens or even hundreds scattered throughout the skeleton. They’re like raindrops hitting a pond, spread widely and densely. In contrast, **Lytic Metastatic Carcinoma (LMC)** usually has **fewer lesions**, and they tend to be more **localized**—clustered in certain areas rather than evenly spread.

**(ii) Shape of lesion outlines**  
The **shape** of the lesions gives another clue. In MM, the edges are usually **round or slightly oval**—think of clean, circular holes punched out of the bone. In LMC, the outlines are more **irregular**, with **denticulations** (tooth-like projections) and **scallops**, giving a jagged, uneven appearance.

**(iii) Size of lesions**  
In MM, individual lesions are generally **small to medium-sized**—up to a few millimeters—though they can grow larger if they merge. In LMC, the size is **more variable**, ranging from small to **very large**—up to several centimeters. So, if you see a big, ragged hole in the bone, LMC becomes more likely.

**(iv) Macroscopic edge appearance**  
When viewed with the naked eye (not under a microscope), MM lesions often have **sharp, well-defined edges**, looking like they were **"punched out"** or **"bored"** into the bone—clean and precise. LMC lesions, on the other hand, have **scalloped, denticulated, or craggy** edges—rough and irregular, like the edge

paper.

**(v) Radiographic appearance**  
On X-rays, MM lesions are **clearly and sharply delimited**—you can draw a neat circle around them. They stand out distinctly from the surrounding healthy bone. LMC lesions, however, appear **obscure, cloudy, or "moth-eaten"**—as if tiny insects have nibbled away at the bone in a scattered, irregular pattern. This "moth-eaten" appearance is a classic sign of aggressive, infiltrative destruction.

**(vi) Surface of surrounding bone**  
In MM, the **surface of the bone around the lesion is typically smooth**—no additional changes. But in LMC, the surrounding bone may be **pitted with tiny additional apertures**. These small holes represent areas where the disease is slowly spreading outward, merging with the main lesion. This creates a **zone of potential expansion**, like a stain spreading on fabric.

**(vii) Osteoblastic (bone-forming) reaction**  
The body sometimes tries to repair damage by laying down new bone. This is called an **osteoblastic reaction**. In **rapidly progressing MM**, this repair response is **absent or extremely slight**—the disease moves too fast for the body to react. But in **LMC**, there can be a **slight to significant** osteoblastic reaction, visible both **macroscopically** (as thickened or dense edges) and **radiographically** (as a rim of increased density around the lesion). This difference reflects the often slower, more chronic nature of metastatic carcinoma compared to aggressive myeloma.

**(viii) Topographic predilection (preferred locations)**  
While both diseases affect similar regions, some **subtle preferences** have been noted. MM tends to favor the **scapula** (especially the glenoid fossa, axillary border, and acromion), the **lateral part of the clavicle**, and the **radius and ulna**.
